chunks: From him, from his father, from Sa'd ibn Abdillah, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, and from Hammad, from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

I asked him, 'How did Ibn Abi Layla rule?' He said, 'I said: He ruled in one issue with four different opinions. [The issue is] regarding the woman whose husband dies, and her family and his family come regarding the household goods (mata'). So he ruled in it according to the saying of Ibrahim al-Nakha'i: Whatever was the household goods of the man, it is for the man; and whatever was the household goods of the women, it is for the woman; and whatever was household goods that belonged to both the man and the woman, he divided it between them into two halves. Then he abandoned this opinion and said: The woman is like a guest in the house of the man. And if a man hosted a man and he claimed the household goods of his house, he would make him provide evidence. And similarly, the woman is made to provide evidence; otherwise, the household goods are for the man. And he returned to another opinion and said: Indeed, the ruling is that the household goods are for the woman, unless the man establishes evidence regarding what he introduced/created in her house. Then he abandoned this opinion and returned to the first opinion of Ibrahim.'

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'The final ruling is that the household goods are for the woman, unless the man establishes evidence. We know those between her two sides (meaning between the two mountains of Mina) that the woman is married off to her husband's house with household goods, and we at that time were in Mina.'

key_terms.إِبْرَاهِيمُ النَّخَعِيُّ: Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, a famous Tabi'i jurist
key_terms.ابْنُ أَبِي لَيْلَى: Ibn Abi Layla, a prominent early Islamic judge
key_terms.جَبَلَا مِنًى: The two mountains of Mina, a geographical reference in Mecca

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic legal ruling on household goods ownership after a husband's death according to Ibn Abi Layla's final judgment?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) uses the evolving judicial opinions of the prominent Sunni judge Ibn Abi Layla to illustrate the principle of *al-qada' al-akhir* (the final ruling prevails), even if the judge later reverted to an earlier view. This narration highlights the Shia scholarly emphasis on customary practice (*urf*) and the specific context of Mina, where brides traditionally brought their household goods, as a key evidentiary basis for determining ownership in marital property disputes.
